performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
question: How can a major-key song feel like a temptation, not a consolation?
intro: A tree by a well, remembered as a place of rest, is the cycle’s first song in a major key. Its gentle tune is broken by a verse of cold wind, and the singer ends far from the tree, still hearing it call.

sections.label: Verses 1–2 · the tree by the well
Verse 3 · into the dark, in the minor

cues.title: The first major key
cues.text: Seven bars for piano alone, marked Mässig, in 3/4, open with a rippling sixteenth-note figure in E major. After four minor-key songs this is the cycle’s first in the major, a change that Peter Gülke, cited on German Wikipedia, compares to a shock.
cues.evidence: The tempo marking, the time signature, the key signature of four sharps and a voice entry in bar 8 after seven piano bars are in the OpenScore transcription (CC0). The keys of songs 1–4 are from the table in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterreise; Gülke’s remark is cited in https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am_Brunnen_vor_dem_Tore. The report’s opening windows are −20.1 dB at 0:00 and −14.5 dB at 0:05; no audio timing of the key is claimed.

cues.title: The well and the gate
cues.text: At the well by the gate stands a linden tree. In its shade he dreamed many a sweet dream, and he carved many a loving word into its bark, drawn back to it in joy and in sorrow. In Müller’s day the linden was a tree where lovers met.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 5, first two stanzas (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. They are sung in bars 8–24 of the score (OpenScore), about 0:22–1:13 by proportion; the voice enters at about 0:20 (boundary novelty 0.41). German Wikipedia (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am_Brunnen_vor_dem_Tore), citing Susan Youens, gives the linden as a tree of love and a meeting place for lovers.

cues.title: Into the dark, then the branches
cues.text: At about 1:14, after piano alone and a drop in level, the key signature loses three sharps and the third verse begins in the minor. At about 1:49 four sharps return for the branches’ call, in one of the song’s loudest windows.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:14 (novelty 0.50) with the quiet windows at 1:10 and 1:20 (−21.6 and −20.0 dB); loudest windows include 1:50 (−10.4 dB), and a boundary at 2:04 (0.70) follows. In the score the voice rests in bars 25–27, the key signature changes from four sharps to one at bar 25 and back to four at bar 37 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: Eyes shut in the dark
cues.text: Tonight he must pass the tree again, deep in the night, and he shuts his eyes in the dark. Then the branches rustle as if calling to him: come here to me, friend, here you will find your rest.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 5, third and fourth stanzas (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. They are sung in bars 28–44 of the score (OpenScore), about 1:22–2:13 by proportion.

cues.title: The song Schober liked
cues.text: When Schubert sang the cycle to his friends, Schober said that only “Der Lindenbaum” had pleased him. Schubert replied that these songs pleased him more than all the rest, and that in time they would please his friends as well. His friend Spaun recalled the scene.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Winterreise article, “Opinions of Schubert’s intentions”, quoting Spaun’s account (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterreise).

cues.title: Notes outside the key
cues.text: From about 2:16 the fifth verse leaves the key: a low C in the piano bass and C naturals in the voice lie outside E major. The strongest boundary, at 2:34, marks the end of the verse.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 2:16 (0.99), 2:28 (0.89) and 2:34 (1.00). The score’s verse 5 (bars 45–53) has a C in the piano bass in bars 45 and 47 and C naturals in the voice in bars 50–52, outside E major (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: The cold wind
cues.text: The cold winds blow straight into his face and his hat flies off his head. He does not turn round.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 5, fifth stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. It is sung in bars 45–53 of the score (OpenScore), about 2:13–2:40 by proportion.

cues.title: Far from the tree
cues.text: Now he is many hours from that place, and he still hears the tree rustle: you would find rest there.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 5, sixth stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. It is sung from bar 58 of the score (OpenScore), about 2:52 by proportion, and a boundary falls at 2:48 (novelty 0.75).

cues.title: The last line three times
cues.text: The last line, “du fändest Ruhe dort”, is sung three times, in bars 64–66, 72–74 and 74–76 of the score. The loudest window of the song, at about 3:30, comes in the repeat.
cues.evidence: The loudest 5-second window is 3:30 (−9.3 dB), with 3:15 also among the loudest. In the score the last line “du fändest Ruhe dort” is sung in bars 64–66, 72–74 and 74–76 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

cues.title: A song for four voices
cues.text: In 1846 Friedrich Silcher arranged Schubert’s first verse for four unaccompanied male voices. Through school and choir songbooks it became the folk song “Am Brunnen vor dem Tore”, and many who know the tune do not know it is Schubert’s. Silcher’s strophic version repeats one melody and loses the later change of tone.
cues.evidence: German Wikipedia, Am Brunnen vor dem Tore, “Silchers Satz” (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am_Brunnen_vor_dem_Tore): Silcher’s 1846 setting for four male voices, based on Schubert’s first strophe, and its spread through school and choir songbooks; Arnold Feil’s remark is cited there.

cues.title: The opening returns
cues.text: From about 3:49 the piano plays its opening figure again, with the rippling sixteenth notes of the first bars, and the song ends in E major. Listen for the last chord, and for how the recording’s level falls away around it.
cues.evidence: The windows at 3:40 and 3:50 are quiet (−24.9 and −24.2 dB), though the final decay is quieter still. The score repeats the opening bars in bars 77–82, with the voice silent (OpenScore); times are proportioned. The pitch of the transfer is uncertain (Utz, footnote 73, https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx).

transitions.title: Three bars of piano, then the minor
transitions.from: Verses 1–2 · the tree by the well
transitions.to: Verse 3 · into the dark, in the minor
transitions.how: The first two verses end in E major. The piano plays three bars alone, and the key signature drops from four sharps to one. The third verse begins in the minor: the same walking pace, but the colour is cold, as the singer passes the tree in the dark. No chord links the two keys; the piano interlude is the pause between them.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:14 (novelty 0.50); the level falls to −21.6 dB at 1:10. In the score the voice rests in bars 25–27 and the key signature changes from four sharps to one at bar 25 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

transitions.title: The branches rustle, the major returns
transitions.from: Verse 3 · into the dark, in the minor
transitions.how: The fourth verse follows the third without a pause. At bar 37 the key signature returns to four sharps, the voice rises on the call of the branches and the piano keeps its figure. The minor of the third verse is, in effect, a shadow that passes: the tree’s own music comes back, now as an invitation.
transitions.evidence: The level reaches −10.4 dB at 1:50. In the score the key signature returns to four sharps at bar 37 and the third verse ends in bar 36 (OpenScore); the time is proportioned.

transitions.title: Notes outside the key
transitions.how: The fifth verse enters straight after the fourth, with no change of signature but a change of harmony. A low C in the piano bass and C and G naturals in the voice bring notes foreign to E major, the cold wind in the singer’s face. The piano’s figure continues, but its notes are distorted, and the tune loses its folk-like shape.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 2:04 (novelty 0.70), 2:16 (0.99) and 2:28 (0.89). The score has a C in the bass in bars 45 and 47 and C naturals in the voice in bars 50–52, outside E major (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

transitions.title: A pause, and the tree again
transitions.how: The cold-wind verse ends, the strongest boundary in the song, and four bars of piano alone fall in level. The final verse then begins in the major, now distant: the singer is hours from the tree, but he hears it still. The tune of the opening returns, and its last line is repeated three times, as a memory that cannot be silenced.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary is 2:34 (1.00); the level is −22.6 dB at 2:40, with a boundary at 2:48 (0.75). In the score the voice rests in bars 54–57 and the last verse enters at bar 58 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

transitions.title: The introduction comes back
transitions.how: After the last “du fändest Ruhe dort”, the piano repeats the rippling figure of the introduction. The song ends as it began, in E major, and the tree is still there; the singer is not. The same music that opened the song becomes its farewell, quieter than before, and the recording ends on a soft chord.
transitions.evidence: The windows at 3:40 and 3:50 are quiet (−24.9 and −24.2 dB). The score repeats the introduction’s opening in bars 77–82 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

source.title: Schubert, Winterreise No. 5, Der Lindenbaum, OpenScore Lieder transcription (CC0)
source.locator: bars 1–82; the voice is silent in bars 1–7, 25–27, 54–57 and 77–82; times proportioned to the boundaries at 0:20, 1:14, 2:16, 2:34 and 2:48.

The last verse, its last line sung three times.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The recording appears to sing all six strophes; no source consulted states the performing text or the key of the transfer. Utz classifies recordings by transposition from the first edition, but the value for this song and the absolute pitch of the transfer are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ES 384, and the Commons file name and the Internet Archive description agree.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CK 2950, take 2 (run-out “Ck 2950” with II); side No. 5 (label number 0942028); reverse side: Wasserflut (matrix CK 2951-2). Disc 3 of 12 of the set; 30 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (256.00 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (255.88 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.
